claim: SMS2 variants p.Ile62Ser and p.Met64Arg are linked to the most severe bone phenotypes in OP-CDL patients.
source: However, the most severe phenotypes are associated with two closely localized missense variants, p.Ile62Ser and p.Met64Arg.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript text based on clinical observations.

claim: SMS2 variants p.Ile62Ser and p.Met64Arg retain full enzymatic activity.
source: Here, we show that SMS2 variants linked to the most severe bone phenotypes retain full enzymatic activity but fail to leave the ER owing to a defective autonomous ER export signal.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that these variants can synthesize SM.

claim: SMS2 variants p.Ile62Ser and p.Met64Arg fail to leave the ER owing to a defective autonomous ER export signal.
source: Here, we show that SMS2 variants linked to the most severe bone phenotypes retain full enzymatic activity but fail to leave the ER owing to a defective autonomous ER export signal.
evidence: This is demonstrated through microscopy showing ER retention of these variants.

claim: Cells harboring pathogenic SMS2 variants accumulate sphingomyelin in the ER.
source: Cells harboring pathogenic SMS2 variants accumulate sphingomyelin in the ER and display a disrupted transbilayer sphingomyelin asymmetry.
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data and SM reporter imaging.

claim: Cells harboring pathogenic SMS2 variants display a disrupted transbilayer sphingomyelin asymmetry.
source: Cells harboring pathogenic SMS2 variants accumulate sphingomyelin in the ER and display a disrupted transbilayer sphingomyelin asymmetry.
evidence: This is demonstrated using cytosolic SM reporters that show SM accessibility on the cytosolic leaflet.

claim: Aberrant sphingomyelin distributions caused by pathogenic SMS2 variants are accompanied by imbalances in cholesterol organization.
source: These aberrant sphingomyelin distributions also occur in patient-derived fibroblasts and are accompanied by imbalances in cholesterol organization, glycerophospholipid profiles, and lipid order in the secretory pathway.
evidence: This is supported by cholesterol reporter experiments and mβCD sensitivity assays.

claim: Aberrant sphingomyelin distributions caused by pathogenic SMS2 variants are accompanied by imbalances in glycerophospholipid profiles.
source: These aberrant sphingomyelin distributions also occur in patient-derived fibroblasts and are accompanied by imbalances in cholesterol organization, glycerophospholipid profiles, and lipid order in the secretory pathway.
evidence: This is demonstrated by lipidomics showing changes in PC and PE levels and saturation.

claim: Aberrant sphingomyelin distributions caused by pathogenic SMS2 variants are accompanied by imbalances in lipid order in the secretory pathway.
source: These aberrant sphingomyelin distributions also occur in patient-derived fibroblasts and are accompanied by imbalances in cholesterol organization, glycerophospholipid profiles, and lipid order in the secretory pathway.
evidence: This is measured using solvatochromic probes NR12A and NRERCl.

claim: The IXMP motif in SMS2 is part of an autonomous ER export signal.
source: This indicates that the IXMP motif in SMS2 is part of an autonomous ER export signal.
evidence: This is demonstrated by chimera experiments showing that the IXMP-containing region can mediate ER export when transferred to SMSr.

claim: Ile62 and Met64 are part of a conserved sequence motif, IXMP, which is located 13–14 residues upstream of the first membrane span in both SMS1 and SMS2.
source: Ile62 and Met64 are part of a conserved sequence motif, IXMP, which is located 13–14 residues upstream of the first membrane span in both SMS1 and SMS2 (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence alignment in Figure 1B.

claim: SMS2I62S and SMS2M64R were each retained in the ER, in contrast to wildtype SMS2, which localized to the Golgi and PM.
source: In agreement with our previous findings (Pekkinen et al., 2019), SMS2I62S and SMS2M64R were each retained in the ER, in contrast to wildtype SMS2, which localized to the Golgi and PM (Figure 1C; Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy showing colocalization with ER marker calnexin.

claim: SMSr-SMS211-77 localized to the Golgi.
source: Contrary to SMSr, SMSr-SMS211-77 localized to the Golgi.
evidence: This is shown by microscopy in Figure 1D.

claim: SMSr-SMS211-77 variants in which Ile62 or Met64 was replaced with Ser or Arg, respectively, were retained in the ER.
source: However, SMSr-SMS211-77 variants in which Ile62 or Met64 was replaced with Ser or Arg, respectively, were retained in the ER (Figure 1D; Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy showing colocalization with ER marker.

claim: Doxycycline-induced expression of SMS2I62S and SMS2M64R, but not their enzyme-dead isoforms, fully restored SM biosynthesis in ΔSMS1/2 cells.
source: This revealed that doxycycline-induced expression of SMS2I62S and SMS2M64R, but not their enzyme-dead isoforms, fully restored SM biosynthesis in ΔSMS1/2 cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown by metabolic labeling with clickable sphingosine and TLC analysis.

claim: Removal of SMS1 and SMS2 wiped out the entire cellular SM pool.
source: Quantitative mass spectrometric analysis of total lipid extracts from wildtype and ΔSMS1/2 cells revealed that removal of SMS1 and SMS2 wiped out the entire cellular SM pool and caused a fourfold increase in glycosphingolipid (GSL) levels, consistent with a competition between Golgi-resident SM and glucosylceramide (GlcCer) synthases for ceramide substrate (Figure 2D; Figure 2—source data 2; Appendix 1—figure 3A, B; Appendix 1—figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC-MS/MS lipidomics.

claim: Removal of SMS1 and SMS2 caused a fourfold increase in glycosphingolipid (GSL) levels.
source: Quantitative mass spectrometric analysis of total lipid extracts from wildtype and ΔSMS1/2 cells revealed that removal of SMS1 and SMS2 wiped out the entire cellular SM pool and caused a fourfold increase in glycosphingolipid (GSL) levels, consistent with a competition between Golgi-resident SM and glucosylceramide (GlcCer) synthases for ceramide substrate (Figure 2D; Figure 2—source data 2; Appendix 1—figure 3A, B; Appendix 1—figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC-MS/MS lipidomics.

claim: In ΔSMS1/2 cells transduced with pathogenic SMS2I62S or SMS2M64R, addition of doxycycline fully restored the SM pool.
source: In ΔSMS1/2 cells transduced with pathogenic SMS2I62S or SMS2M64R, addition of doxycycline fully restored the SM pool.
evidence: This is shown by mass spectrometry data in Figure 2D.

claim: ΔSMS1/2 cells expressing SMS2I62S or SMS2M64R contained three- to fourfold higher levels of dihydroceramide (Cer d18:0/16:0) and dihydroceramide-based SM (SM d18:0/16:0) than wildtype or SMS2-expressing ΔSMS1/2 cells.
source: Moreover, ΔSMS1/2 cells expressing SMS2I62S or SMS2M64R contained three- to fourfold higher levels of dihydroceramide (Cer d18:0/16:0) and dihydroceramide-based SM (SM d18:0/16:0) than wildtype or SMS2-expressing ΔSMS1/2 cells (Figure 2D; Figure 2—source data 2; Appendix 1—figure 3B; Appendix 1—figure 3—source data 1), which suggests that ER-resident pathogenic SMS2 variants compete with ceramide desaturase DES1 for dihydroceramide substrate synthesized in the ER.
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC-MS/MS lipidomics.

claim: ER-resident pathogenic SMS2 variants compete with ceramide desaturase DES1 for dihydroceramide substrate synthesized in the ER.
source: Moreover, ΔSMS1/2 cells expressing SMS2I62S or SMS2M64R contained three- to fourfold higher levels of dihydroceramide (Cer d18:0/16:0) and dihydroceramide-based SM (SM d18:0/16:0) than wildtype or SMS2-expressing ΔSMS1/2 cells (Figure 2D; Figure 2—source data 2; Appendix 1—figure 3B; Appendix 1—figure 3—source data 1), which suggests that ER-resident pathogenic SMS2 variants compete with ceramide desaturase DES1 for dihydroceramide substrate synthesized in the ER.
evidence: This is inferred from the accumulation of dihydroceramide and dihydroSM.

claim: The ER from ΔSMS1/2 cells expressing SMS2 had a lipid composition similar to that of the ER from wildtype cells.
source: The ER from ΔSMS1/2 cells expressing SMS2 had a lipid composition similar to that of the ER from wildtype cells.
evidence: This is shown by shotgun lipidomics of purified ER.

claim: The ER from SMS2M64R-expressing cells contained sevenfold higher SM levels, that is ~10 mol% SM instead of ~1.5 mol% of all identified lipids.
source: In contrast, the ER from SMS2M64R-expressing cells contained sevenfold higher SM levels, that is ~10 mol% SM instead of ~1.5 mol% of all identified lipids (Figure 3D; Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by shotgun lipidomics of purified ER.

claim: The increase in ER-bound SM caused by SMS2M64R was accompanied by a twofold rise in DAG levels.
source: This increase in ER-bound SM was accompanied by a twofold rise in DAG levels and a significant drop in the amount of PC and ceramide, consistent with the presence of a catalytically active SM synthase in the ER.
evidence: This is shown by lipidomics data in Figure 3D.

claim: The increase in ER-bound SM caused by SMS2M64R was accompanied by a significant drop in the amount of PC and ceramide.
source: This increase in ER-bound SM was accompanied by a twofold rise in DAG levels and a significant drop in the amount of PC and ceramide, consistent with the presence of a catalytically active SM synthase in the ER.
evidence: This is shown by lipidomics data in Figure 3D.

claim: Expression of SMS2M64R led to a marked (1.8-fold) increase in ER-associated PE levels.
source: Interestingly, expression of SMS2M64R also led to a marked (1.8-fold) increase in ER-associated PE levels.
evidence: This is shown by lipidomics data in Figure 3D.

claim: Expression of SMS2M64R enhanced unsaturation of bulk phospholipid in the ER, as indicated by a significant rise in di-unsaturated PC at the expense of saturated and mono-unsaturated PC species.
source: However, we noticed that expression of SMS2M64R enhanced unsaturation of bulk phospholipid in the ER, as indicated by a significant rise in di-unsaturated PC at the expense of saturated and mono-unsaturated PC species (Figure 3E; Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of PC species in purified ER.

claim: SMS2M64R expression caused a sharp increase in ER-bound ceramide-1-phosphate (Cer1P).
source: Strikingly, SMS2M64R expression also caused a sharp increase in ER-bound ceramide-1-phosphate (Cer1P; Figure 3D; Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is shown by lipidomics data in Figure 3D.

claim: Cellular Cer1P levels were essentially abolished in SM synthase-deficient cells.
source: Moreover, cellular Cer1P levels were essentially abolished in SM synthase-deficient cells, indicating that production of Cer1P is tightly coupled to SM biosynthesis.
evidence: This is shown by lipidomics data comparing wildtype and ΔSMS1/2 cells.

claim: Production of Cer1P is tightly coupled to SM biosynthesis.
source: Moreover, cellular Cer1P levels were essentially abolished in SM synthase-deficient cells, indicating that production of Cer1P is tightly coupled to SM biosynthesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Cer1P is absent in SMS-deficient cells.

claim: The PM from ΔSMS1/2 cells expressing SMS2M64R had a slightly reduced SM content (~8 mol%) even though the total SM content of these cells was considerably higher.
source: In comparison, the PM from ΔSMS1/2 cells expressing SMS2M64R had a slightly reduced SM content (~8 mol%) even though the total SM content of these cells was considerably higher (Figure 4D; Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by shotgun lipidomics of purified PM.

claim: The PM from ΔSMS1/2 cells expressing SMS2M64R contained fourfold higher levels of dihydroSM.
source: In addition, the PM from ΔSMS1/2 cells expressing SMS2M64R contained fourfold higher levels of dihydroSM (represented by SM species with 0 double bonds; Figure 4E; Figure 4—source data 2), consistent with the ER residency of this enzyme.
evidence: This is shown by analysis of SM species in purified PM.

claim: Upon co-expression with SMS2M64R, EqtSMSS but not EqtSolSS displayed a distinct punctate distribution that coincided with the ER network.
source: However, upon co-expression with SMS2M64R, EqtSMSS but not EqtSolSS displayed a distinct punctate distribution that coincided with the ER network.
evidence: This is shown by microscopy in Figure 5A.

claim: EqtSMSS-containing puncta were not observed in cells expressing the enzyme-dead variant SMS2M64R/D276A.
source: EqtSMSS-containing puncta were not observed in cells expressing the enzyme-dead variant SMS2M64R/D276A, indicating that their formation strictly relies on SM production in the ER (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy showing no puncta formation with the catalytically inactive variant.

claim: After incubation for 5 min in hypotonic medium, the ER's fine tubular network transformed into numerous micrometer-sized vesicles.
source: After incubation for 5 min in hypotonic medium, the ER's fine tubular network transformed into numerous micrometer-sized vesicles.
evidence: This is shown by microscopy in Figure 5B.

claim: In SMS2M64R-expressing cells, the membranes of ER-derived vesicles were extensively labelled with EqtSMSS.
source: In SMS2M64R-expressing cells, the membranes of these ER-derived vesicles were extensively labelled with EqtSMSS (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy of hypotonically swollen cells.

claim: In hypotonic cells co-expressing EqtSMSS with SMS2M64R/D276A or EqtSolSS with SMS2M64R, the reporter was found exclusively in the lumen of ER-derived vesicles.
source: In contrast, in hypotonic cells co-expressing EqtSMSS with SMS2M64R/D276A or EqtSolSS with SMS2M64R, the reporter was found exclusively in the lumen of ER-derived vesicles, indicating that Eqt staining of the ER membrane critically relies on catalytically active SMS2M64R and a SM-binding competent reporter.
evidence: This is shown by microscopy in Figure 5B.

claim: Expression of pathogenic variant SMS2I62S or SMS2M64R in each case caused EqtSMcyto to accumulate in numerous puncta that were dispersed throughout the cytosol.
source: In contrast, expression of pathogenic variant SMS2I62S or SMS2M64R in each case caused EqtSMcyto to accumulate in numerous puncta that were dispersed throughout the cytosol (Figure 6A; Appendix 1—figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy showing cytosolic puncta formation.

claim: Formation of EqtSMcyto puncta required expression of a catalytically active pathogenic variant.
source: Formation of these puncta required expression of a catalytically active pathogenic variant and was not observed when using SM binding-defective cytosolic reporter EqtSolcyto (Appendix 1—figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy with enzyme-dead variants and non-binding reporters.

claim: Cells expressing pathogenic SMS2 variants mobilized GFP-tagged LysSMcyto to cytosolic puncta that colocalized extensively with mKate-tagged EqtSMcyto.
source: Cells expressing pathogenic SMS2 variants mobilized GFP-tagged LysSMcyto to cytosolic puncta that colocalized extensively with mKate-tagged EqtSMcyto (Figure 6B, C; Appendix 1—figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-localization microscopy.

claim: The EqtSMcyto-positive puncta in SMS2I62S or SMS2M64R-expressing cells largely segregated from a wide range or organellar markers.
source: Remarkably, the EqtSMcyto-positive puncta in SMS2I62S or SMS2M64R-expressing cells largely segregated from a wide range or organellar markers, including VAPA (ER), Sec16L (ER exit sites), ERGIC-53 (cis-Golgi), GM130 (medial-Golgi), TGN64 (trans-Golgi), EEA1 (early endosomes), LAMP1 (lysosomes), and LD540 (lipid droplets; Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: This is shown by co-staining with various organellar markers.

claim: EqtSMcyto-positive puncta displayed considerable overlap with EqtSMSS-positive puncta formed in the ER lumen of SMS2M64R-expressing cells.
source: However, EqtSMcyto-positive puncta displayed considerable overlap with EqtSMSS-positive puncta formed in the ER lumen of SMS2M64R-expressing cells (Figure 6D, upper row), suggesting that the former originate at least in part from the ER.
evidence: This is shown by co-localization microscopy.

claim: Upon hypotonic swelling, the EqtSMSS-positive puncta became largely continuous with the ER membrane and segregated from the EqtSMcyto-positive puncta.
source: Upon hypotonic swelling, the EqtSMSS-positive puncta became largely continuous with the ER membrane and segregated from the EqtSMcyto-positive puncta (Figure 6D, bottom row).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy of hypotonically swollen cells.

claim: Under hypotonic conditions, EqtSMcyto-positive puncta gave rise to small vesicular structures.
source: Under these conditions, EqtSMcyto-positive puncta gave rise to small vesicular structures, implying the presence of a membranous core.
evidence: This is observed by microscopy in Figure 6D.

claim: Wildtype cells could be readily stained with the SM reporter EqtSM whereas ΔSMS1/2 cells were devoid of EqtSM staining.
source: As shown in Figure 7A, wildtype cells could be readily stained with the SM reporter whereas ΔSMS1/2 cells were devoid of EqtSM staining.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy and flow cytometry.

claim: Expression of SMS2, but not enzyme-dead SMS2D276A, restored EqtSM staining of ΔSMS1/2 cells to a level approaching that of wildtype cells.
source: Expression of SMS2, but not enzyme-dead SMS2D276A, restored EqtSM staining of ΔSMS1/2 cells to a level approaching that of wildtype cells.
evidence: This is shown by microscopy and flow cytometry in Figure 7A, B.

claim: Expression of SMS2M64R restored cell surface staining to only a minor degree even though the PM-associated SM pool of these cells was close to that of wildtype or SMS2-expressing ΔSMS1/2 cells.
source: In contrast, expression of SMS2M64R restored cell surface staining to only a minor degree (Figure 7A, B) even though the PM-associated SM pool of these cells was close to that of wildtype or SMS2-expressing ΔSMS1/2 cells (Figure 4D; Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing EqtSM staining with lipidomics data.

claim: The lipid order reported by NR12A in the outer PM leaflet of SM-deficient ΔSMS1/2 cells was drastically reduced in comparison to that of wildtype cells.
source: As expected, the lipid order reported by NR12A in the outer PM leaflet of SM-deficient ΔSMS1/2 cells was drastically reduced in comparison to that of wildtype cells (Figure 7C, D - Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ratiometric imaging with NR12A probe.

claim: Expression of SMS2 partially restored lipid order in the outer PM leaflet.
source: Expression of SMS2 partially restored lipid order.
evidence: This is shown by NR12A ratiometric imaging in Figure 7C, D.

claim: Expression of SMS2M64R failed to restore lipid order in the outer PM leaflet to any appreciable degree.
source: In contrast, expression of SMS2M64R failed to restore lipid order to any appreciable degree.
evidence: This is shown by NR12A ratiometric imaging in Figure 7C, D.

claim: The lipid order reported by NRERCl in SMS2M64R-expressing cells was significantly enhanced in comparison to that of SMS2-expressing cells.
source: Conversely, the lipid order reported by NRERCl in SMS2M64R-expressing cells was significantly enhanced in comparison to that of SMS2-expressing cells (Figure 7E, F - Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ratiometric imaging with NRERCl probe.

claim: Cytosolic D4H-mCherry primarily stained the inner PM leaflet in wildtype HeLa cells.
source: Accordingly, we found that cytosolic D4H-mCherry primarily stained the inner PM leaflet in wildtype HeLa cells.
evidence: This is shown by microscopy in Appendix 1—figure 6A.

claim: Cytosolic D4H-mCherry displayed a more diffuse cytosolic distribution in ΔSMS1/2 cells.
source: In contrast, the probe displayed a more diffuse cytosolic distribution in ΔSMS1/2 cells (Appendix 1—figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy.

claim: Expression of SMS2 in ΔSMS1/2 cells restored PM staining by D4H-mCherry.
source: Expression of SMS2 inΔSMS1/2 cells restored PM staining, indicating that PM-associated SM is critical for controlling the reporter-accessible cholesterol pool in the inner PM leaflet (Appendix 1—figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy.

claim: In ΔSMS1/2 cells expressing pathogenic variant SMS2M64R or SMS2I62S, cytosolic D4H-mCherry did not label the inner PM leaflet but primarily accumulated on intracellular vesicles.
source: Strikingly, in ΔSMS1/2 cells expressing pathogenic variant SMS2M64R or SMS2I62S, cytosolic D4H-mCherry did not label the inner PM leaflet but primarily accumulated on intracellular vesicles that were largely segregated from EqtSMcyto-positive puncta (Figure 8A; Appendix 1—figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy.

claim: D4H-positive vesicles in cells expressing pathogenic SMS2 variants co-localized extensively with dextran-positive endolysosomal compartments.
source: These vesicles co-localized extensively with dextran-positive endolysosomal compartments (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is shown by co-localization microscopy.

claim: ΔSMS1/2 cells displayed a substantially reduced tolerance for mβCD in comparison to wildtype cells.
source: As expected, ΔSMS1/2 cells displayed a substantially reduced tolerance for mβCD in comparison to wildtype cells (Figure 8C; Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell viability assays.

claim: Expression of SMS2 restored mβCD tolerance of ΔSMS1/2 cells to that of wildtype cells.
source: Expression of SMS2 restored mβCD tolerance of ΔSMS1/2 cells to that of wildtype cells.
evidence: This is shown by cell viability assays in Figure 8C.

claim: Expression of SMSM64R or SMS2I62S in each case failed to render ΔSMS1/2 cells resistant toward mβCD.
source: In contrast, expression of SMSM64R or SMS2I62S in each case failed to render ΔSMS1/2 cells resistant toward mβCD.
evidence: This is shown by cell viability assays in Figure 8C.

claim: In patient fibroblasts the membranes of ER-derived vesicles were extensively labelled with EqtSMSS.
source: Strikingly, in patient fibroblasts the membranes of ER-derived vesicles were extensively labelled with EqtSMSS (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy of hypotonically swollen patient fibroblasts.

claim: In fibroblasts of healthy controls, EqtSMSS was found exclusively in the lumen of ER-derived vesicles.
source: In contrast, in fibroblasts of healthy controls, EqtSMSS was found exclusively in the lumen of ER-derived vesicles.
evidence: This is shown by microscopy in Figure 9A.

claim: The cytosolic SM reporter EqtSMcyto accumulated in numerous puncta when expressed in patient fibroblasts.
source: In addition, we found that the cytosolic SM reporter EqtSMcyto accumulated in numerous puncta when expressed in patient fibroblasts while its expression in fibroblasts of healthy controls resulted in a diffuse cytosolic distribution (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy.

claim: Expression of EqtSMcyto in fibroblasts of healthy controls resulted in a diffuse cytosolic distribution.
source: In addition, we found that the cytosolic SM reporter EqtSMcyto accumulated in numerous puncta when expressed in patient fibroblasts while its expression in fibroblasts of healthy controls resulted in a diffuse cytosolic distribution (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy.

claim: Aberrant SM distributions in patient fibroblasts were accompanied by significant alterations in lipid order on the cell surface.
source: Interestingly, these aberrant SM distributions were accompanied by significant alterations in lipid order on the cell surface (Figure 9C) and in the ER (Figure 9D; Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ratiometric imaging with NR12A probe.

claim: Aberrant SM distributions in patient fibroblasts were accompanied by significant alterations in lipid order in the ER.
source: Interestingly, these aberrant SM distributions were accompanied by significant alterations in lipid order on the cell surface (Figure 9C) and in the ER (Figure 9D; Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ratiometric imaging with NRERCl probe.

claim: In patient fibroblasts, a substantial portion of the D4H-mCherry reporter was shifted to intracellular vesicles.
source: Moreover, while the cytosolic cholesterol reporter D4H-mCherry primarily stained the PM of fibroblasts of healthy controls, in patient fibroblasts a substantial portion of the reporter was shifted to intracellular vesicles (Appendix 1—figure 7).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy.

claim: SM is a dominant sphingolipid in mammalian cells.
source: Sphingomyelin is a dominant sphingolipid in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: SM production in the trans-Golgi traps cholesterol synthesized in the ER to promote formation of a sphingomyelin/sterol gradient along the secretory pathway.
source: Its production in the trans-Golgi traps cholesterol synthesized in the ER to promote formation of a sphingomyelin/sterol gradient along the secretory pathway.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of SM-cholesterol interactions.

claim: The sphingomyelin/sterol gradient marks a fundamental transition in physical membrane properties that help specify organelle identify and function.
source: This gradient marks a fundamental transition in physical membrane properties that help specify organelle identify and function.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of membrane biophysics.

claim: Mutations in sphingomyelin synthase SMS2 cause osteoporosis and skeletal dysplasia.
source: We previously identified mutations in sphingomyelin synthase SMS2 that cause osteoporosis and skeletal dysplasia.
evidence: This was reported in a previous publication by the authors.

claim: Eukaryotic membranes consist of complex lipid mixtures, with amounts and ratios of the individual lipids showing marked variations between organelles and membrane leaflets.
source: Eukaryotic membranes consist of complex lipid mixtures, with amounts and ratios of the individual lipids showing marked variations between organelles and membrane leaflets (van Meer et al., 2008; Harayama and Riezman, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Lipid-induced changes in bilayer-thickness, lipid packing density and surface charge accompany the transition from early to late organelles in the secretory pathway.
source: Particularly striking are the lipid-induced changes in bilayer-thickness, lipid packing density and surface charge that accompany the transition from early to late organelles in the secretory pathway (Bigay and Antonny, 2012; Holthuis and Menon, 2014; Sharpe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: These changes in membrane properties are highly conserved across species.
source: These changes are highly conserved across species and provide specific cues for membrane proteins that govern vital processes such as protein secretion and signaling (Bigay and Antonny, 2012; Magdeleine et al., 2016; Zhou and Hancock, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The bulk of SM is synthesized in the lumen of the trans-Golgi from ceramides supplied by the ER.
source: The bulk of SM is synthesized in the lumen of the trans-Golgi from ceramides supplied by the ER and delivered by vesicular transport to the PM, where it accumulates in the exoplasmic leaflet (Hanada et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SM is the preferred binding partner of cholesterol.
source: SM is the preferred binding partner of cholesterol (Slotte, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: About one-third of the total cholesterol pool in the PM is sequestered by SM.
source: About one-third of the total cholesterol pool in the PM is sequestered by SM (Das et al., 2014; Endapally et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SM biosynthesis in mammals is mediated by SM synthase 1 (SMS1) and SMS2.
source: SM biosynthesis in mammals is mediated by SM synthase 1 (SMS1) and SMS2.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: SMS1 and SMS2 act as phosphatidylcholine (PC):ceramide phosphocholine transferases.
source: Both enzymes act as phosphatidylcholine (PC):ceramide phosphocholine transferases, which catalyze the transfer of the phosphorylcholine head group from PC onto ceramide to generate SM and diacylglycerol (DAG) (Huitema et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SMS1 resides in the trans-Golgi.
source: SMS1 resides in the trans-Golgi, and its deficiency in mice causes mitochondrial dysfunction and disrupts insulin secretion (Yano et al., 2013; Yano et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SMS2 resides both in the trans-Golgi and at the PM.
source: SMS2 resides both in the trans-Golgi and at the PM.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: SMS2 deficiency ameliorates diet-induced obesity and insulin resistance.
source: Its deficiency ameliorates diet-induced obesity and insulin resistance (Kim et al., 2018; Li et al., 2011; Mitsutake et al., 2011; Sugimoto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SMS2 is highly expressed in bone.
source: We previously reported that SMS2 is highly expressed in bone and identified heterozygous mutations in the SMS2-encoding gene (SGMS2) as the underlying cause of a clinically described autosomal dominant genetic disorder – osteoporosis with calvarial doughnut lesions (OP-CDL: OMIM #126550) (Pekkinen et al., 2019).
evidence: This was reported in a previous publication by the authors.

claim: Heterozygous mutations in SGMS2 are the underlying cause of osteoporosis with calvarial doughnut lesions (OP-CDL).
source: We previously reported that SMS2 is highly expressed in bone and identified heterozygous mutations in the SMS2-encoding gene (SGMS2) as the underlying cause of a clinically described autosomal dominant genetic disorder – osteoporosis with calvarial doughnut lesions (OP-CDL: OMIM #126550) (Pekkinen et al., 2019).
evidence: This was reported in a previous publication by the authors.

claim: The milder OP-CDL phenotype is associated with the nonsense variant p.Arg50*.
source: The milder phenotype is associated with the nonsense variant p.Arg50*, which gives rise to a truncated but catalytically active enzyme that mislocalizes to the cis/medial-Golgi (T. Sokoya and J. Holthuis, unpublished data).
evidence: This is based on unpublished data from the authors.

claim: The nonsense variant p.Arg50* gives rise to a truncated but catalytically active enzyme that mislocalizes to the cis/medial-Golgi.
source: The milder phenotype is associated with the nonsense variant p.Arg50*, which gives rise to a truncated but catalytically active enzyme that mislocalizes to the cis/medial-Golgi (T. Sokoya and J. Holthuis, unpublished data).
evidence: This is based on unpublished data from the authors.

claim: Missense variants p.Ile62Ser and p.Met64Arg enhance de novo SM biosynthesis by blocking ER export of enzymatically active SMS2.
source: Interestingly, these missense variants enhance de novo SM biosynthesis by blocking ER export of enzymatically active SMS2 (Pekkinen et al., 2019).
evidence: This was reported in a previous publication by the authors.

claim: OP-CDL in patients with pathogenic SMS2 variants is not due to a reduced capacity to synthesize SM but rather a consequence of mistargeting bulk SM production to an early secretory organelle.
source: This suggests that OP-CDL in patients with pathogenic SMS2 variants is not due to a reduced capacity to synthesize SM but rather a consequence of mistargeting bulk SM production to an early secretory organelle.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that pathogenic variants retain enzymatic activity but are mislocalized.

claim: Pathogenic SMS2 variants profoundly undermine the cellular capacity to uphold nonrandom lipid distributions in the secretory pathway.
source: Our data indicate that pathogenic SMS2 variants profoundly undermine the cellular capacity to uphold nonrandom lipid distributions in the secretory pathway that may be critical for the bone forming activity of osteogenic cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the comprehensive data presented in the study.

claim: Nonrandom lipid distributions in the secretory pathway may be critical for the bone forming activity of osteogenic cells.
source: Our data indicate that pathogenic SMS2 variants profoundly undermine the cellular capacity to uphold nonrandom lipid distributions in the secretory pathway that may be critical for the bone forming activity of osteogenic cells.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the observed effects of pathogenic variants.

claim: Cells harboring pathogenic SMS2 variants retain the ability to concentrate cholesterol in the PM and keep their ER levels low in spite of a dissipated SM gradient.
source: However, we now find that cells harboring pathogenic SMS2 variants retain the ability to concentrate cholesterol in the PM and keep their ER levels low in spite of a dissipated SM gradient.
evidence: This is demonstrated by lipidomics data showing similar cholesterol levels in PM and ER.

claim: Pathogenic SMS2 variants had no impact on the cellular pool of cholesteryl esters.
source: However, pathogenic SMS2 variants had no impact on the cellular pool of cholesteryl esters.
evidence: This is shown by lipidomics data.

claim: The oxysterol binding protein OSBP mediates net transfer of cholesterol from the ER to the trans-Golgi by counter transporting phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate (PI4P).
source: An alternative mechanism involves the oxysterol binding protein OSBP, which mediates net transfer of cholesterol from the ER to the trans-Golgi by counter transporting phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate (PI4P), a lipid continuously produced in the trans-Golgi and turned over in the ER (Mesmin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The cholesterol/PI4P exchange activity of OSBP influences membrane lipid order in the secretory pathway.
source: As critical determinant of intracellular cholesterol flows, the cholesterol/PI4P exchange activity of OSBP also influences membrane lipid order in the secretory pathway (Mesmin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The ER lacks transport systems to efficiently distribute SM to other organelles in sync with its rate of synthesis.
source: In contrast, the PM-like SM content of the ER in cells harboring pathogenic SMS2 variants indicates that such mechanism does not exist for SM and that the ER lacks transport systems to efficiently distribute this lipid to other organelles in sync with its rate of synthesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the accumulation of SM in the ER when SMS2 is mislocalized.

claim: ER-resident scramblases display low specificity, with phospholipids and sphingolipids being translocated with similar kinetics.
source: These scramblases display low specificity, with phospholipids and sphingolipids being translocated with similar kinetics (Buton et al., 2002; Chalat et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SM produced by pathogenic SMS2 variants in the ER lumen should readily equilibrate with the cytosolic leaflet.
source: Consequently, SM produced by pathogenic SMS2 variants in the luminal leaflet of the ER should readily equilibrate with the cytosolic leaflet.
evidence: This is inferred from the known activity of ER scramblases.

claim: Cells expressing SMS2M64R had similar levels of SM in the PM as controls but showed a significantly reduced SM reporter staining of their surface.
source: Moreover, cells expressing SMS2M64R had similar levels of SM in the PM as controls but showed a significantly reduced SM reporter staining of their surface, indicative of a perturbed SM asymmetry across the PM.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing lipidomics data with EqtSM staining.

claim: Cells harboring pathogenic SMS2 variants displayed a reduced PM staining with a cytosolic sterol reporter that recognizes free cholesterol but not cholesterol sequestered by SM.
source: Consistent with an elevated SM pool in the cytosolic leaflet, cells harboring pathogenic SMS2 variants displayed a reduced PM staining with a cytosolic sterol reporter that recognizes free cholesterol but not cholesterol sequestered by SM.
evidence: This is shown by D4H reporter experiments.

claim: The dramatic rise in ER-associated SM levels caused by pathogenic SMS2 variants was accompanied by a marked increase in PC desaturation.
source: The dramatic rise in ER-associated SM levels caused by pathogenic SMS2 variants was accompanied by a marked increase in PC desaturation and a nearly twofold expansion of the PE pool.
evidence: This is shown by lipidomics analysis of purified ER.

claim: The dramatic rise in ER-associated SM levels caused by pathogenic SMS2 variants was accompanied by a nearly twofold expansion of the PE pool.
source: The dramatic rise in ER-associated SM levels caused by pathogenic SMS2 variants was accompanied by a marked increase in PC desaturation and a nearly twofold expansion of the PE pool.
evidence: This is shown by lipidomics analysis of purified ER.

claim: An enhanced desaturation and rise in cone-shaped, ethanolamine-containing phospholipids may be part of an adaptive cellular response to counter an SM-mediated rigidification of the ER bilayer.
source: While it remains to be established how these alterations are implemented, it is conceivable that an enhanced desaturation and rise in cone-shaped, ethanolamine-containing phospholipids are part of an adaptive cellular response to counter an SM-mediated rigidification of the ER bilayer and preserve the organelle's central role in membrane biogenesis and secretion.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed lipid changes.

claim: Cer1P is produced by ceramide kinase CERK.
source: Cer1P is produced by ceramide kinase CERK and functions as a key signaling lipid in the regulation of cell growth, survival and inflammation (Presa et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Cer1P functions as a key signaling lipid in the regulation of cell growth, survival and inflammation.
source: Cer1P is produced by ceramide kinase CERK and functions as a key signaling lipid in the regulation of cell growth, survival and inflammation (Presa et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The nonsense pathogenic SMS2 variant p.Arg50* is more common in patients with OP-CDL and associated with a milder bone phenotype.
source: While this study focuses on the impact of the missense SMS2 variants p.M64R and p.I62S on the subcellular organization of SM, the nonsense pathogenic SMS2 variant p.Arg50* is more common in patients with OP-CDL and associated with a milder bone phenotype (Mäkitie et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Met64 in the p.Arg50* variant is utilized as alternative start codon, yielding a truncated but catalytically active enzyme that is mislocalized to the cis/medial Golgi.
source: However, our recent work revealed that Met64 in the p.Arg50* variant is utilized as alternative start codon, yielding a truncated but catalytically active enzyme that is mislocalized to the cis/medial Golgi (T. Sokoya and J. Holthuis, unpublished data).
evidence: This is based on unpublished data from the authors.

claim: SMS2R50X would have no direct access to ER-derived ceramides and must compete with GlcCer synthase for ceramides delivered to the cis/medial Golgi.
source: Unlike pathogenic variants SMS2I62S and SMS2M64R, SMS2R50X would have no direct access to ER-derived ceramides and must compete with GlcCer synthase for ceramides delivered to the cis/medial Golgi.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization of SMS2R50X to the cis/medial Golgi.

claim: Backflow of SM produced in the cis/medial Golgi to the ER may affect the lipid landscape in the secretory pathway of cells expressing SMS2R50X, but to a lesser extent than that observed in cells expressing the pathogenic variants SMS2I62S and SMS2M64R.
source: Backflow of SM produced in the cis/medial Golgi to the ER may affect the lipid landscape in the secretory pathway of cells expressing SMS2R50X, but to a lesser extent than that observed in cells expressing the pathogenic variants SMS2I62S and SMS2M64R.
evidence: This is a speculative comparison based on the different localizations of the variants.

claim: SMS2 transcript levels are highest in cortical bone and vertebrae.
source: A quantitative analysis of SMS2 transcript levels in a murine tissue panel revealed the highest expression in cortical bone and vertebrae (Pekkinen et al., 2019).
evidence: This was reported in a previous publication by the authors.

claim: The impact of pathogenic SMS2 variants on the lipid composition of secretory organelles will be most severe in bone cells of the affected individuals.
source: This implies that the impact of pathogenic SMS2 variants on the lipid composition of secretory organelles will be most severe in bone cells of the affected individuals.
evidence: This is inferred from the high expression of SMS2 in bone.

claim: Pathogenic variants of core components of COPII-coated vesicles cause craniofacial and skeletal defects by selectively disrupting procollagen export from the ER.
source: Interestingly, pathogenic variants of core components of COPII-coated vesicles have been reported to cause craniofacial and skeletal defects by selectively disrupting procollagen export from the ER (Boyadjiev et al., 2006; Garbes et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Loss of TANGO1 results in neonatal lethality due to insufficient bone mineralization.
source: Moreover, loss of TANGO1, an ER-resident transmembrane protein required for packaging the bulky procollagen fibers into COPII vesicles, results in neonatal lethality due to insufficient bone mineralization (Guillemyn et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: ER export of procollagen may be particularly susceptible to the bilayer rigidifying effect of SM synthesized by pathogenic SMS2 variants.
source: It is conceivable that ER export of procollagen is particularly susceptible to the bilayer rigidifying effect of SM synthesized by pathogenic SMS2 variants.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the known effects of SM on membrane properties.

claim: Bone mineralization critically relies on neutral SMase-2 (SMPD3).
source: Bone mineralization critically relies on neutral SMase-2 (SMPD3), another membrane-bound enzyme highly expressed in bone that cleaves SM in the cytosolic leaflet of the PM to generate ceramide and phosphocholine (Aubin et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: nSMase-2 gains access to SM upon SM scrambling by the Ca2+-activated scramblase TMEM16F.
source: nSMase-2 gains access to SM upon SM scrambling by the Ca2+-activated scramblase TMEM16F (Niekamp et al., 2022).
evidence: This was reported in a previous publication by the authors.

claim: Loss of TMEM16F leads to decreased mineral deposition in skeletal tissues.
source: Loss of TMEM16F leads to decreased mineral deposition in skeletal tissues (Ehlen et al., 2013), suggesting that this process may require a TMEM16F-mediated supply of exoplasmic SM to nSMase-2 for SM hydrolysis in the cytosolic leaflet.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Bone mineralization may require a TMEM16F-mediated supply of exoplasmic SM to nSMase-2 for SM hydrolysis in the cytosolic leaflet.
source: Loss of TMEM16F leads to decreased mineral deposition in skeletal tissues (Ehlen et al., 2013), suggesting that this process may require a TMEM16F-mediated supply of exoplasmic SM to nSMase-2 for SM hydrolysis in the cytosolic leaflet.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the role of TMEM16F.

claim: By disrupting SM asymmetry, pathogenic SMS2 variants may interfere with a coordinated release of the lipid-based phosphate store, thus impairing normal bone mineralization.
source: By disrupting SM asymmetry, pathogenic SMS2 variants may interfere with a coordinated release of the lipid-based phosphate store, thus impairing normal bone mineralization.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism of disease.
